1 big thing: Trump, Big AI all-in together
 
Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images

President Trump and the AI industry have co-signed one of the biggest economic and technological wagers of all time, Axios' Zachary Basu writes.

  • If it goes right: a new age of abundance — explosive productivity, staggering wealth and a generational leap in American power.
  • If it goes wrong: a catastrophic bust that destroys capital, jobs and, in the words of several involved, threatens widespread human harm.

Why it matters: Neither Trump nor the AI titans have plausible deniability. Their fortunes have become so tightly bound that success will be shared — and failure impossible to disown.

🖼️ The big picture: Trump and Big AI have fused their futures around four enormous bets.

1. The economic bet: Trillions poured into chips, data centers and power will create a productivity engine powerful enough to fuel a new Industrial Revolution.

  • AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach $10.3 trillion by 2032, but the payoff remains unproven: one analysis found hyperscalers have spent nearly $1 trillion more on AI since 2024 than AI has generated in revenue.
  • The promise sold by Trump and his tech allies: a new era of growth and abundance. The peril: a historic misallocation of capital on a scale few industries have ever seen.

2. The regulation bet: Washington can clear the runway for an AI takeoff while leaving the companies largely responsible for policing themselves.

  • The new White House accord signed by Trump and the AI giants enshrines voluntary safeguards, company-led testing and third-party reviews instead of new federal mandates.
  • The promise: American dominance over China. The peril: Self-regulation fails, forcing Washington to intervene only after damage has already been inflicted.

3. The safety bet: AI can grow vastly more powerful without becoming vastly harder to control.

  • Many of the most dire safety warnings come from AI researchers themselves. Anthropic's own IPO prospectus contemplates scenarios in which advanced AI kills humanity.
  • The promise is almost limitless: superintelligent systems that help cure diseases and accelerate scientific discovery. The peril: self-improving AI that evolves faster than its creators can comprehend or contain.

4. The political bet: Trump and Big AI can become inseparable without making each other even more toxic.

  • Trump has staked his legacy on winning the AI race, dismissing fears about data centers costing Republicans in the midterms. The industry has staked billions on the policy environment he's creating.
  • The promise: Trump and Big AI become partners in this century's defining technological transformation. The peril: Every AI failure, disruption or backlash becomes a liability they share.

The bottom line: Trump and the AI industry are asking the country for a leap of faith at a time when polls show Americans lack faith in both.

2. 🪖 "Shark Tank" for military bases
 
Pete Hegseth gives a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico. Photo: Alex Wong/Getty Images

In a sweeping hourlong address to hundreds of junior officers and enlisted leaders at Quantico, Va., Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth proposed a pitch-off between states to see who should host America's newest military base, Axios' Thomas Novelly writes.

  • "If your state wants the honor of hosting 15- to 25,000 of America's great troops, show us why and how you're going to do it," Hegseth said.

The big picture: New military infrastructure is a major economic driver for states and can lead to political tugs-of-war, like the yearslong fight between Colorado and Alabama to claim U.S. Space Command's headquarters.

  • America's newest military installation is Colorado's Schriever Space Force Base, which was opened in 1985.

More details.

Palmer Luckey, Newt Gingrich and Elon Musk at Sec. Hegseth's Quantico address yesterday. Screenshot: DOD/via X

Hegseth also announced "Project Meridian," a Pentagon study of the future of warfare led by Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich, Axios' Colin Demarest writes.

  • It's Musk's first official role advising the Trump administration since his very public feud last year with President Trump after departing DOGE.

Meridian, Hegseth said, will examine "the domains we must conquer, and capabilities we must master."

3. 🧽 AI tries to shed toxic branding
 
Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images

The great AI rebranding is on, led by President Trump and tech titans like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who are embracing an alternative term: "Superintelligence," or SI, Axios' Dave Lawler writes.

  • Why it matters: Leaders in D.C. and Silicon Valley are worried that public backlash against AI and data centers will hamper the development of this staggeringly powerful and existentially dangerous technology.

Flanked by the most powerful figures in tech, Trump on Tuesday declared "superintelligence" the preferred terminology of the executive branch.

  • Huang has extended the label to physical infrastructure, referring to data centers as "superintelligence factories."

Some of the tech executives who appeared with Trump continued to use "AI" in their remarks. SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk caught himself and pivoted to "SI." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has long used the "superintelligence" branding.

4. 🤠 Texas group spends over $100M in two weeks
 
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton speaks to the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas on Sept. 9. Photo: Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images

A new Texas PAC spent a staggering $131 million in just 17 days to boost struggling Republican Ken Paxton in his Senate battle, and tens of millions more could be on the way, Axios' Marc Caputo writes from new financial reports.

  • Texas PAC, created last month, is affiliated with the GOP Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC for Senate Republicans.

Why it matters: This is a race where money may not make the difference. In a "craptastic" environment for GOP candidates nationwide, Paxton's many scandals have left him particularly vulnerable.

  • One analyst said on X: "The election version of the Battle of Verdun, folks."

🗳️ Zoom out: Paxton, the state attorney general, could well become the first Republican to lose a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. In polls, he's tied or behind Democratic state Rep. James Talarico, a seminarian who has cast Paxton and Republicans as corrupt and beholden to billionaires.

  • As of Monday, Talarico was on track to be outspent nearly 5-to-1 by pro-Paxton groups in the campaign's final two months, The New York Times reports.

💰 Zoom in: Texas PAC filed an FEC report yesterday showing the group had just spent more than $61.4 million in two days on ads and other activities for Paxton and against Talarico.

  • That brought the PAC's total spending on Paxton's behalf to more than $131 million in 17 days — more than $7.7 million a day.

Democrats backing Talarico are unlikely to come close to GOP spending, but are stepping up their ad buys.

5. 🥾 Scoop: Rubio kicked out Iranian delegation
 
Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during a UN Security Council meeting in New York last week. Photo: Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images

Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanded on Monday that the Iranian delegation to the UN General Assembly immediately leave the country after negotiations stalled, a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter told Axios' Barak Ravid.

  • Why it matters: Though the Iranians were likely to depart soon anyway, Rubio's move was a highly unusual diplomatic rebuke and laid bare the deep distrust between the two countries amid fruitless efforts to broker an end to the war.

Qatari mediators tried to secure a diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran but made little progress, with neither side willing to budge.

  • Among those ordered to leave New York was Rubio's Iranian counterpart, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

6. 🤑 The AI wealth effect
 
Data: Federal Reserve. (Includes securities held indirectly through mutual funds, defined-contribution pension plans and variable life insurance/annuity products.) Chart: Emily Peck/Axios

Americans' wealth jumped by $12.8 trillion in the second quarter, led by a nearly $11 trillion gain in stock holdings and other financial assets, Axios Markets author Emily Peck writes from new Fed data.

  • That's the biggest single quarterly increase, in dollar terms, on record.

🛍️ What's happening: The AI boom-fueled wealth surge is propelling spending in the U.S. economy.

  • Half of all growth in consumption is being driven by those effects, says Krishna Guha, head of economics at Evercore ISI.

7. ✈️ Heroic plumber helped save plane
 
Assaf Regavim, one of the passengers who stormed the cockpit to stop the attacking pilot, speaks to reporters outside the terminal at Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Airport. Photo: Erik Marmor/Getty Images

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described on CNN how passengers helped rescue a FlyDubai flight bound for Israel that plunged after Capt. Smit Machchhar was stabbed by his co-pilot, Axios' Rebecca Falconer writes.

  • An Israeli passenger who works as a plumber, Yaniv Hayun, entered the cockpit and found the Omani co-pilot at the controls, the Israeli prime minister told CNN's Jim Sciutto. Machchhar had unlocked the cockpit after being attacked.

Hayun pulled back on the aircraft's controls, while another passenger and crew member subdued the attacker. Off-duty FlyDubai pilots then took over and stabilized the plane.

  • Netanyahu said the attacker, an Omani national, was arrested in Saudi Arabia and was undergoing interrogation there. His motive was unclear.

8. 🎨 Hidden masterpieces hit auction
 
Claude Monet's 'Le Jardin des Tuileries' on display during a preview of the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection at Sotheby's in London. Photo: Ben Bauer/PA Images via Getty Images

A dozen Impressionist and post-Impressionist artworks collectively valued at almost half a billion dollars are going up for auction after sitting unseen for decades in South America.

  • Works by Vincent van Gogh and Paul Cézanne are expected to smash records for the artists in the Nov. 18 sale in New York, AP reports.

The paintings come from a collection amassed by the late Argentine art collector Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her sugar magnate husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier.

  • They include van Gogh's landscape "Châtaigniers en fleurs" (Chestnut Trees in Flower), estimated at $180 million, and Cézanne's portrait "Arlequin," estimated at $120 million.
  • Neither has been seen in public for half a century.
